title: Man blackmails people posing as YouTube employee, nabbed
notes: Delhi Police arrested a man who befriended victims on social media, recorded them in compromising WhatsApp video calls, then posed as a YouTube employee and as a Delhi Police cyber crime inspector, demanding money not to upload the footage. One complainant paid over Rs 25 lakh across multiple transactions.

title: Avoid unknown video calls: Cyber police warn amid rising sextortion cases
publisher: The Hitavada (Bhopal Cyber Crime Police advisory)
notes: Bhopal Cyber Crime police advisory: criminals build trust through fake social media and dating-app profiles, record obscene video calls, then threaten to send the material to family and friends. Advises rejecting unknown video calls, not paying blackmailers because payment does not end the demands, preserving evidence and reporting to 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in.

title: MHA think tank alerts against hijack, sextortion scams on social media
notes: Reports a BPRD (MHA police think tank) advisory on WhatsApp frauds: unknown video calls used for nude-recording sextortion; account hijacking where the takeover account asks the victim's contacts for money; and impersonation of a CEO/senior officer using a fake profile to demand urgent payments, citing a new number or an important meeting. Advises 2FA and not answering unknown calls.

title: A new scam on the rise: Strangers stripping on video calls to extort money
notes: Describes nude video-call recording via dating apps, Facebook and Sharechat, sometimes using morphed footage; follow-up calls from a fake Superintendent of Police claiming the woman attempted or died by suicide and a case would be filed, and fake YouTube staff offering to delete the video for a fee. Victims paid in repeated instalments; quotes Rachakonda police warnings.

title: Cyber Crime Cell issues advisory against fake calls
publisher: The Goan (Goa Police Cyber Crime Cell advisory)
notes: Goa Police Cyber Crime Cell warned of 'virtual kidnapping' calls, often from foreign or VPN numbers, telling parents their child was kidnapped, in an accident or in police custody and demanding money for release. Advises staying calm, verifying directly with the child, not sending money, and reporting to police and Sanchar Saathi.

title: Rangat woman loses Rs 2.7 lakh in online fraud after fake police call about her son being involved in rape case
notes: A caller posing as police said the woman's son was named in a rape case and would be arrested, with a voice resembling her son in the background, and demanded money to settle with officers and the victim's family; she paid Rs 2.7 lakh in multiple transfers. Police stressed that they do not take money to drop cases.

title: Fraudsters targeting families of students
notes: Fake police called parents of Chandigarh school students claiming the child was held in a drug case, put a crying girl on the line, told the parent not to hang up and demanded Rs 50,000 for release. Police advised verifying callers, never paying unfamiliar numbers and reporting to 1930.

title: Kapurthala farmer loses Rs 11.75 lakh in cyber fraud
notes: Callers told a Punjab couple their son in Canada had caused a serious accident, then posed as officials warning of legal consequences, claimed the son's phone was with police and told them not to contact him; they transferred Rs 11.75 lakh from two bank accounts without telling anyone.

title: Defending Against Frontier AI Driven Cyber Risks (CIAD-2026-0020)
notes: High-severity CERT-In advisory on AI-enabled cyber risks. For individuals it warns that AI-generated deepfakes and impersonation can be highly convincing and advises verifying voice calls, video messages and urgent requests, especially where money or sensitive information is involved. It does not detail family-impersonation scripts.

title: Tamil Nadu Police cybercrime advisory on AI voice cloning
publisher: MediaNama (Tamil Nadu Police Cyber Crime Wing advisory)
notes: Tamil Nadu Cyber Crime Wing warned that scammers harvest voice samples from social media videos or 'wrong number' calls, clone the voice with AI, then call the person's contacts in a distressed tone asking for urgent money via UPI. Advises probing questions, verifying identity through a known channel and reporting to 1930.

title: Family member in distress or an AI voice clone? The rise of a disturbing new cyber crime scam
notes: Describes a Noida mother who paid Rs 60,000 by UPI after a call in her son's cloned voice saying he was under threat; she later noticed he used an unfamiliar form of address. Experts advise calling back on a known number and agreeing family code words; cites a McAfee survey that 66% of Indian respondents would likely respond to urgent money calls from relatives.

title: When your voice is no longer proof
notes: Opinion piece citing a Kolkata case where a 67-year-old sent Rs 95,990 within an hour to a caller who cloned an acquaintance's voice and claimed a relative was hospitalised. Notes there is no separate national figure for AI voice-clone fraud and repeats the government's 'Pause, Verify, Report' advice and 1930 helpline.

title: Matrimonial fraud: MHA I4C warns of fake profiles on marriage sites (Hindi)
notes: Reports an I4C (MHA) warning that fraudsters create fake matrimonial profiles posing as NRIs, doctors, engineers, army officers or businessmen, build emotional bonds and propose quickly, then ask for money for customs duty on gifts, travel/visa costs or emergencies. Red flags include avoiding video calls and emotional pressure; advises no money transfers before meeting, reverse image search and reporting to 1930.

title: 2 Nigerians dupe women on pretext of marriage, arrested
notes: Men posing as UK-based marine engineers contacted women on marriage websites, shared a flight ticket, then a woman posing as a Mumbai airport official said the 'groom' was detained with foreign currency and needed customs clearance fees; one victim paid about Rs 4 lakh in several payments.

title: I4C detects two latest cyber crime trends in India
publisher: ETV Bharat (reporting I4C National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit advisory)
notes: I4C's threat analytics unit flagged fake profiles on matrimonial and dating platforms (Shaadi.com, Jeevansathi, Tinder, Bumble) posing as well-off NRIs or armed-forces personnel, filtering targets by age and income, building trust via calls and WhatsApp video, then creating urgent situations to push money or fake crypto investments. Advises reverse image search and not sending money to people not met in person.

title: Delhi Police arrest man who duped women via dating apps and matrimonial sites
publisher: Kerala Kaumudi (Delhi Police cyber cell case)
notes: Delhi Police cyber cell arrested a man who posed as a doctor, businessman, film producer or lawyer on dating apps, matrimonial sites and Instagram, spent months building emotional connections with women, then asked for money citing medical emergencies, business losses or family problems; police said about Rs 2 crore was taken from over 500 women.

title: Techie catfished of Rs 81.67 lakh, 2 arrested
notes: Andhra Pradesh police arrested two people after a software employee met a woman on Instagram who claimed to be in love with him, gradually gained his trust and allegedly took Rs 81.67 lakh from him.

title: App date turns costly for civil services aspirant
notes: A Tinder match invited a man to a Delhi cafe for her 'birthday', left early, and the cafe presented a bill of about Rs 1.22 lakh; he was threatened and forced to pay online. Police said the bill was split between the woman, managers and owners and described a wider scheme in metro cities, noting stigma stops victims reporting.

title: CBIC mounting multi-modal awareness against frauds in name of Customs
publisher: Kashmir Reader (reporting Ministry of Finance / CBIC release)
notes: Reports the Finance Ministry/CBIC awareness campaign: fraudsters posing as courier staff or Customs/Police/CBI officials claim a parcel or gift from abroad is held and demand duty or clearance fees, sometimes alleging contraband. CBIC states Customs officers never call, SMS or email asking for duty into private accounts, and genuine communications carry a verifiable DIN; report at cybercrime.gov.in or 1930.

title: Kerala woman duped of Rs 12 lakh in customs scam: Government reveals how this fraud works
notes: Reports a PIB Fact Check warning that Indian Customs never calls or SMSes asking for duty to be paid into personal bank accounts, and a Kerala woman who lost Rs 12 lakh after paying an initial Rs 15,000 'duty' on a gift and then escalating amounts. PIB quote: Indian Customs never call/SMS to pay duty in personal accounts.

title: Nigerian cheats Kottayam woman, loots money; arrested in Delhi
notes: A fake Facebook friend 'from the UK' told a housewife a valuable gift was sent; a caller posing as a diplomatic agent at Mumbai Customs demanded Rs 22,000 duty, followed by more 'customs officers' at other airports who threatened legal action; she sold gold and took loans, losing Rs 81 lakh to named bank accounts.

title: Diglipur woman duped of Rs 5.22 lakh by cyber fraudsters
notes: A Facebook friend posing as a UK benefactor moved the chat to WhatsApp and said gifts had reached Delhi Airport; a fake customs official demanded release fees, and the woman paid Rs 5.22 lakh via Google Pay to personal bank accounts before a further Rs 4.99 lakh demand alerted her.

title: OLX / Quikr QR code fraud
notes: Delhi Police describes fraudsters posing as Army/paramilitary personnel who agree to buy a seller's item, claim a remote posting means they can only pay online, send a fake payment screenshot, then send QR codes and have the seller enter the UPI PIN, debiting the seller repeatedly with ever larger 'correction' amounts. Advises verifying identity, avoiding advance payments and not scanning QR codes to receive money.

title: Cyber frauds exploiting goodwill of security forces to dupe people online
notes: Fraudsters pose as army or paramilitary personnel on OLX and Quikr, offering cheap vehicles or goods because they are 'transferred', sending fake service ID cards and asking for small advances; others send QR codes or payment links that debit sellers. Notes a CISF public warning on 4 Sep 2020 and advises not dealing with anyone who only shows an unverified official ID.

title: OLX scams on the rise again in Tamil Nadu, customers fall prey to fake 'army men'
notes: Buyer-side variant: a fake army officer lists a scooter or car, claims a transfer, sends an ID card, insists on advance payment by Google Pay because outsiders cannot enter the camp, then demands more money. Tamil Nadu cyber crime cell reported about 100 such complaints since January 2020.

title: Public advisory on fraudsters using armed forces personnel details to perpetrate financial cyber frauds
publisher: Nicobar Times (Andaman and Nicobar Police advisory)
notes: Andaman and Nicobar Police warned that fraudsters misuse Indian Army personnel identities to target people advertising property for rent on housing platforms and social media. Advises verifying prospective renters separately, being wary of urgency, and remembering OTPs/PINs are needed to send money, not to receive it.

title: Hyderabad man loses over Rs 12.75 lakh in house rental cyber fraud
publisher: The Week (PTI, citing Hyderabad Cyber Crime Police)
notes: A flat owner who listed on a real-estate portal was called by a fake NSG commando 'being transferred' and his 'senior officer', who cited a special defence security protocol requiring him to pay first to 'raise a demand' for an Rs 80,000 advance; he lost Rs 12.75 lakh in IMPS/UPI transfers. Police warned of Army/NSG impersonation targeting property owners with forged IDs.

title: Fraudsters posing as Army personnel and invoking nationalism execute unique crime in Hyderabad
notes: A fake Army officer tenant using 'Jai Hind' messaging had an 'Army accountant' ask a Secunderabad owner to send Rs 5 as a 'reversal mode' test (returned to build trust), then the advance and repeated amounts so the 'system' would credit them back; she lost Rs 1.3 lakh. Police warned not to blindly believe people claiming to be from the Army.

title: KBC lottery fraud
notes: WhatsApp messages, mostly from +92 numbers, claim the recipient won Rs 25 lakh in a KBC-Jio lottery and must contact a 'manager', who asks for refundable processing charges and GST into various bank accounts, keeps 'raising' the prize and demands more for weeks. Notes genuine lotteries deduct tax from the prize, warns against callers who insist on secrecy and against skipping a talk with family.

title: Lottery scam
notes: Describes lottery/prize and commission emails, SMS and calls where victims are drawn in gradually and asked to pay transfer fees, taxes or transport costs in stages, money going to offshore or Indian carrier accounts. Advises never responding to fake lottery wins and never sending money to unknown people for promised returns.

title: Social media crimes
notes: Lists fake/impersonation profiles of known persons, account hacking used to deceive contacts, and 'fake online friendship' scams where fraudsters build an emotional bond and then ask for money citing medical emergencies, legal trouble or problems abroad. Advises refusing strangers' requests and asking platforms to remove fake profiles while warning contacts.

title: Mayabunder resident duped of INR 3,57,000 in KBC lottery scam offering INR 25,00,000 winnings
notes: A resident got a WhatsApp call saying she had won Rs 25 lakh in a KBC lottery, shared bank details, photo and Aadhaar, and paid 'processing fees and taxes' in 14 transactions to multiple bank accounts totalling Rs 3.57 lakh.

title: Kerala Police warns public against fake WhatsApp gift scam using popular brand names
notes: Kerala Police warned of WhatsApp messages using dairy and other well-known brand names and logos to offer 'anniversary gifts' and 'free gifts', with links to fake look-alike company portals that aim to steal money and personal information. Full article partly paywalled.

title: Advisories (I4C advisory listing page)
publisher: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), MHA
notes: Index of I4C/NCTAU public advisories including matrimonial-platform crypto fraud (Oct 2025), 'Boss scam' executive impersonation (Jun 2026), hacked WhatsApp accounts (Jan 2022), army-personnel rental fraud (Jul 2022), travel/holiday fraud (Aug 2021), bogus giveaways (Aug 2021), romance frauds via dating apps (Aug 2021) and KBC lottery frauds (Sep 2021).

title: Misuse of Matrimonial Platforms for Investment/Crypto Frauds (TAU/ADV/006)
publisher: I4C National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit, MHA
notes: Based on NCRP complaint analysis, fraudsters create fake profiles with stolen or morphed photos on Jeevansathi, Shaadi, Matrimony.com and dating apps, pose as professionals abroad, in the armed forces or reputed firms, filter targets by age and income, build intimacy via calls and WhatsApp video (often with edited backgrounds), then create urgent or emotional situations to solicit money or crypto 'investments'. Advises reverse image search and no transfers to people not met in person.

title: Cybercriminals hacking WhatsApp accounts to defraud citizens (Cyber Crime Information-145)
notes: Explains WhatsApp takeover by tricking victims into merging a verification call or sharing the activation OTP, then using the hijacked account to message all contacts and groups with requests like being hospitalised and needing money, plus extortion. Advises two-step verification and that friends and relatives should not respond to money requests from such accounts.

title: Regulatory and Executive Impersonation for WhatsApp Account Takeover using Malicious Windows Executables and High value financial fraud (TAU/ADV/017)
publisher: I4C National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit, MHA
notes: Describes the 'Boss Scam': executives are sent malicious archives posing as urgent RBI/regulatory compliance, which hijack their WhatsApp Web session; fraudsters then message finance staff from the real account (or a number saved as 'CEO') instructing immediate payments to mule accounts. Advises finance teams to verify urgent payment requests by direct voice call or in person.

title: Fraudsters using Army personnel details to perpetrate financial cyber frauds (Cyber Crime Information-159)
notes: From NCRP complaints: fraudsters posing as newly posted Army officials target owners advertising on 99acres, Housing.com and social media, claim the deposit can only be paid via the 'Army bank', ask victims to send small verification amounts and then send UPI 'request money' collects that victims approve thinking they will receive money. States that OTP/PIN entry is for sending money, not receiving.

title: Cybercriminals defrauding citizens going on holiday as travel restrictions ease (Cyber Crime Information-127)
notes: Fraudsters use fake travel ads on social media, impersonate travel agents or airlines offering big discounts, and build fake travel and holiday-accommodation websites misusing names like MakeMyTrip and Airbnb; victims pay and contact stops. Advises checking URLs for slight domain changes and that deals too good to be true usually are.

title: Bogus giveaway scam (Cyber Crime Information-129)
notes: Bogus giveaways of phones, travel packages or crypto are promoted on YouTube, Instagram and SMS; victims are asked to pay a transfer or administrative fee, sometimes on a forged website that also harvests bank details. Advises never paying fees for giveaways.

title: Romance Frauds perpetrated through dating apps (Cyber Crime Information-130)
notes: Fraudsters create fake dating/social-media profiles, use 'love bombing', move the chat off the app to phone or messaging, and once trusted ask for money, gifts, bank details or intimate pictures/videos; often part of criminal networks. Advises not sending money or documents to unknown people.

title: Kaun Banega Crorepati (KBC) Lottery Frauds (Cyber Crime Information-132)
notes: Based on many NCRP complaints: lottery-win images (Rs 25/50/75 lakh) circulate on WhatsApp and Telegram from +92 and other international numbers; callers posing as the 'KBC team' demand a refundable processing amount or GST first, then keep demanding more on new pretexts.

title: Cybercriminals committing Business Partnership scam to defraud citizens (Cyber Crime Information-125)
notes: A fraudster posing as a wealthy foreign investor offers a business partnership in India and promises lakhs to set it up, but first asks the victim to deposit money in various accounts for documentation, customs and other taxes, then disappears.

title: Cybercriminals using fake restaurant websites to defraud citizens (Cyber Crime Information-131)
notes: Fraudsters clone restaurant or fast-food franchise websites; customers pay but nothing arrives and card/bank details are harvested; sites change URLs when reported. Advises ordering only from known sites, checking spelling/domain age and confirming with the business.

title: Comn. & IT Directorate CRPF cyber newsletter: MHA's I4C issues alert on online booking scams targeting pilgrims, tourists
notes: Summarises an I4C nationwide alert on online booking frauds mostly hitting religious pilgrims and tourists: fake websites, social media pages, WhatsApp accounts and sponsored Google/Facebook ads offering Kedarnath helicopter bookings, Char Dham yatra, guest house/hotel stays, cabs and religious tour packages. Also reports a Hyderabad Shaadi.com fake-profile case (Rs 11 lakh plus blackmail).

title: FaceBook SOS frauds
notes: Scammers clone or hijack a real Facebook profile and message the person's friends: an SOS for urgent money for a hospital or accident with repayment promised in a day or two, a fake lottery, or a donation appeal for a needy person. Advises calling the person directly and treating any money request over Messenger as immediately suspect.

title: FaceBook friendship frauds
notes: Fraudsters befriend victims on Facebook or matrimonial sites, move to foreign-code VoIP calls, promise expensive gifts by courier, then a fake Indian Customs caller demands customs charges and GST for cash or jewellery in the parcel, backed by fake receipts and tracking sites; a variant uses a fake ticket and the 'foreigner' detained at the airport. Advises never depositing money on such instructions, even small amounts.

title: Gift card frauds
notes: Fraudsters impersonate the victim's boss or a senior person by email or text and ask them to buy Amazon gift cards and send the claim codes, citing employee incentives, client appreciation or charity, while claiming to be busy, travelling or unreachable so the request cannot be checked. Advises verifying via a known channel and treating urgency as a tell-tale sign.

title: Fake shopping site frauds
notes: Fake shopping sites copy known brands or pose as new stores offering very low prices and take online payment but never deliver, or send used items; a variant promises a free gift and then 'customer service' demands refundable handling or GST fees. Advises suspicion of deep discounts, checking reviews and preferring cash on delivery on untested sites.

title: Cheating scams
notes: Advance-fee lures (lottery wins, money-transfer commissions, overseas jobs, throwaway-price goods, hacked contacts pleading for money) followed by fees, taxes or transport costs. Advises verifying any contact through an independently sourced number and never paying upfront to unknown parties.

title: VHP raises alarm about fake messages on social media soliciting donations in guise of donations for Ram Mandir
notes: Cybercriminals circulated social media messages and calls seeking donations for the Ram Temple with QR codes that sent money to fraudsters; when a VHP worker posed as a donor, the caller asked for a WhatsApp number to send a QR code. VHP complained to MHA and Delhi/UP police and said the temple trust had authorised no fundraising.

title: Cops monitor dubious Ram Mandir links
notes: Hyderabad cybercrime police warned before the Ayodhya consecration about dubious links promising live photos and fraudulent QR codes soliciting donations, cautioning that such links can expose phones and bank accounts.

title: Engineer corners Rs 118 flood aid with fake ID resembling Kerala CM's
notes: A fraudster registered a look-alike UPI ID differing by one letter from the Kerala Chief Minister's Distress Relief Fund ID to catch flood-relief donations; Kerala Police had NPCI/SBI remove it and arrested him in Mumbai. Article notes the difference is hard to spot at a glance.

title: Cyber Crimes Through Fake Sites
publisher: PIB, Ministry of Home Affairs (Rajya Sabha written reply)
notes: MoS Home reply: NCRB does not separately record fake-website frauds; NCRP added a 'Report Suspect' feature (31 Jan 2024) for suspicious URLs (5,252 reported by then) and a facility to check a website's authenticity under 'Suspect Data'; I4C with NIXI disabled 310 malicious .in domains (Oct 2023-May 2024) and 91 phishing/fake websites. Fetched via direct download because WebFetch got 403.

title: I4C cautions corporates and finance professionals against 'Boss Scam': WhatsApp account takeover through malicious 'Statement of Account', 'MCA' and 'RBI' files aimed at high-value financial fraud
notes: I4C reports a sharp rise in NCRP complaints (Delhi, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Rajasthan) of WhatsApp takeover via malicious 'Statement of Account'/RBI/MCA zip files; the hijacked senior executive's account, or a number saved as 'CEO', then instructs finance staff to make urgent transfers to mule accounts. Advises verifying any urgent fund-transfer instruction by direct voice call or in person; says I4C alerted over 58,000 potential victims in 30 days.

title: Sextortion frauds
notes: Criminals using fake profiles on dating apps, matrimonial sites or Instagram build rapport, push for intimate images or sex chats/nude video calls which they record, then demand money (sometimes lakhs) threatening to upload it or send it to family and friends. Advises preserving evidence and filing a police complaint; warns to be wary when someone pushes quickly toward intimacy.

title: Disclaimer (fake websites using the Amul name)
notes: Amul warns that fraudsters use its brand, logo and address on fake websites to deceive the public, and advises people not to send money, personal information or bank details to anyone claiming to represent or be associated with Amul; verify via Amul's business office or www.amul.com. It does not specifically describe franchise fees.

title: Fake government website frauds
notes: Fraudsters create sites imitating government portals and schemes, advertising jobs, subsidies or benefits and collecting registration, examination or verification fees. Advises verifying with the department or PIB Fact Check and not trusting emblems/logos as proof.

title: IRCTC HeliYatra (Shri Kedarnath Dham helicopter booking portal)
notes: Official portal states that helicopter services for the Shri Kedarnath Dham Yatra can be booked only through the IRCTC official website. Fetched via direct download because WebFetch got 403.

title: Spot the Scam Before the Scam Spots You (brochure)
notes: I4C brochure (image PDF, read visually). Sextortion: scammers record private photos or video calls, starting from chats on social media/dating sites or unknown video calls; advice is do not pay and report. WhatsApp scam: a contact's hijacked handle sends an OTP 'by mistake' and asks you to forward it, which hijacks your account. Dating app scam: fake profiles ask for money or push investment, sometimes leading to blackmail.

title: Cyber Surakshini: book on cybercrime against women
notes: I4C awareness book (image PDF, read visually). Online sextortion page advises not engaging or paying because it leads to further demands, and reporting at cybercrime.gov.in/1930. Voice cloning page describes a mother tricked by an AI clone of her son's voice asking for emergency money and advises a family code word and not acting on money requests without confirmation. Romance scam page describes a 'professional working abroad' on a dating platform who avoids meetings or video verification and then claims an emergency.

title: Refund and Recovery Scams
notes: Scammers target people who already lost money (using 'sucker lists'), posing as government agencies, consumer groups, law firms or the original company, and demand upfront retainers, processing fees or taxes to recover the money. FTC states legitimate agencies and organisations do not charge fees to help get refunds or guarantee recovery.

title: Union Home Minister reviews National Cyber Crime Helpline 1930 and directs to make it better
notes: Describes the official route for getting defrauded money back in India: CFCFRMS blocks fraudulent transactions through banks, an MHA SOP (January 2026) coordinates banks and police to return blocked funds, and a Money Restoration Module and Grievance Redressal Module have benefited about one lakh citizens. Fetched via direct download because WebFetch got 403.
